From: Ms. Rivera
Subject: Change to Our Field Trip

Hi everyone,

I have some news about our trip to the Lakeside Nature Center, which was originally planned for Friday, May 9. However, the center called me this morning to explain that a water pipe broke in their main building, and workers need a few days to fix it. Because of this problem, our trip will now take place on Tuesday, May 13.

The bus will still leave from the front of the school at 8:30 a.m., so please arrive at least fifteen minutes early so that we can take attendance. We should return by 2:45 p.m., which is before the last class of the day ends.

If you already turned in your permission form, you do not need to complete a new one. Your parents only need to send me a short note saying that the new date is fine. Students who have not returned the form yet must give it to me by Monday afternoon.

Remember to bring a packed lunch and a water bottle, because the center does not sell any food or drinks. Also, please wear comfortable shoes that can get muddy, since we will be walking along the pond trail.

See you soon,
Ms. Rivera

Maple Street Library: Summer Reading Challenge

This summer, the Maple Street Library invites students ages 11 to 15 to participate in our Summer Reading Challenge, which begins on June 20 and ends on August 15.

How It Works
Sign up at the front desk or on our website, and you will receive a reading log. Each time you finish a book, write its title in your log and ask a librarian to stamp it. Books that are assigned for school do not count, but comic books and audiobooks do.

Prizes
After five stamps, you will get a free bookmark, and after ten stamps, you may choose a paperback book to keep. Every reader who reaches fifteen stamps will be entered in a drawing for a new tablet computer. The winner will be announced at our end-of-summer party on August 22.

Special Events
Every Wednesday at 3:00 p.m., we will hold a book talk in the Community Room, where students may describe a favorite book in three minutes or less. Snacks will be provided.

Questions?
Speak with Mr. Okafor, our teen librarian, or call the library at 555-0142. Please remember that the library is closed on Sundays during the summer months.

Many animals locate food by looking for it. Bats that hunt at night, however, face a serious problem, because it is often too dark to see insects flying through the air. To solve this problem, most of these bats rely on an ability called echolocation.

Echolocation works by using sound. As a bat flies, it produces a series of extremely high-pitched calls, most of which are too high for human ears to detect. When the sound waves hit an object, such as a moth or a tree branch, they bounce back toward the bat. These returning sounds are called echoes. The bat's large ears collect the echoes, and its brain uses them to create a detailed picture of its surroundings.

The echoes provide the bat with a surprising amount of information. The time it takes for an echo to return tells the bat how far away an object is: a quick echo means that the object is close, while a slow echo means that it is farther away. Changes in the echo can also indicate whether an insect is moving toward the bat or away from it, and even how large the insect is.

As a bat approaches its prey, it calls faster and faster. At the beginning of a hunt, a bat might produce about ten calls per second, but in the final moment before it captures an insect, it may produce nearly two hundred. This rapid series of calls, sometimes called a "feeding buzz," allows the bat to follow every sudden turn its prey makes.

Bats are not the only animals that use echolocation. Dolphins and some whales use it underwater, where light does not travel far. Scientists have also studied echolocation in order to design useful tools for people. For example, ships use a system called sonar to measure the depth of the ocean and to locate objects beneath the surface. In this way, an ability that helps a small animal catch its dinner has also helped humans explore the sea.

choices: Why bats are more active at night than during the day

explanation: The passage explains how echolocation works for bats and notes that dolphins, whales, and even ships use similar methods.

Today, most people pay for goods with coins, paper bills, or electronic cards. However, money as we know it has not always existed. For thousands of years, people obtained what they needed through a system called barter.

In a barter system, people exchange goods or services directly. A farmer with extra wheat, for instance, might trade some of it to a potter for a clay pot. This arrangement works well when each person has something the other one wants. But barter has a serious weakness. Imagine that the potter does not need any wheat. The farmer would then have to find someone who wants wheat and who also has something the potter wants, and finding such a match could take days.

To make trading easier, many societies began using particular objects as an early form of money. These objects had to be valued by almost everyone in the community. In different regions of the world, people used shells, salt, cattle, and even enormous stones. Because everyone accepted these items, a farmer could sell wheat for shells and later use the shells to purchase a pot.

Eventually, metal became a popular choice. Metals such as gold, silver, and copper were durable, which meant that they did not rot or break easily, and they could also be divided into smaller pieces for inexpensive purchases. Still, traders had to weigh the metal every time they used it, which was a slow process.

About 2,600 years ago, rulers in the kingdom of Lydia, located in what is now Turkey, solved this problem. They began producing coins that had a standard weight and an official stamp on each one. The stamp showed that the ruler guaranteed the coin's value, so people no longer needed to weigh it. The idea spread quickly to other lands, and coins soon became an ordinary part of daily life.

Ways of trading changed over time, leading to the use of coins.

explanation: The passage moves from barter to objects such as shells, then to metal, and finally to the first coins in Lydia.

In a barter system, people exchange goods or services directly. A farmer with extra wheat, for instance, might trade some of it to a potter for a clay pot. This arrangement works well when each person has something the other one wants. But barter has a serious weakness. Imagine that the potter does not need any wheat. The farmer would then have to find someone who wants wheat and who also has something the potter wants, and finding such a match could take days.

To make trading easier, many societies began using particular objects as an early form of money. These objects had to be valued by almost everyone in the community. In different regions of the world, people used shells, salt, cattle, and even enormous stones. Because everyone accepted these items, a farmer could sell wheat for shells and later use the shells to purchase a pot.

Eventually, metal became a popular choice. Metals such as gold, silver, and copper were durable, which meant that they did not rot or break easily, and they could also be divided into smaller pieces for inexpensive purchases. Still, traders had to weigh the metal every time they used it, which was a slow process.

About 2,600 years ago, rulers in the kingdom of Lydia, located in what is now Turkey, solved this problem. They began producing coins that had a standard weight and an official stamp on each one. The stamp showed that the ruler guaranteed the coin's value, so people no longer needed to weigh it. The idea spread quickly to other lands, and coins soon became an ordinary part of daily life.

choices: The stamp

explanation: The stamp guaranteed "the coin's value, so people no longer needed to weigh it"; "it" is the coin.

Before electric refrigerators were invented, keeping food cold was a genuine challenge. In many places, people depended on natural ice, which was cut from frozen lakes and ponds during the winter months. For a period in the 1800s, this ice became a valuable product that was shipped around the world.

The ice trade began with a Boston businessman named Frederic Tudor. In 1806, he filled a ship with ice and sent it to the Caribbean island of Martinique, where the weather is hot throughout the year. Many people laughed at the plan, because they believed that the ice would simply melt during the long voyage. In fact, much of it did, and Tudor lost money on his first attempts.

However, Tudor did not give up. He experimented with various methods to keep ice from melting, and he discovered that packing the blocks tightly together and surrounding them with sawdust slowed melting considerably. Sawdust, a waste product from lumber mills, was inexpensive and easy to find. It acted as insulation, a material that prevents heat from passing through.

The method of cutting ice also improved. Workers originally used axes and hand saws, which was slow and produced uneven pieces. Later, a horse-drawn tool was invented that cut deep lines across the ice in a grid pattern. This allowed workers to divide the ice into neat blocks of identical size, which were easier to stack and store.

By the middle of the 1800s, ice from New England was traveling as far as India. Cold drinks, fresh fish, and ice cream became possible in places that had never seen frozen water. The trade gradually ended in the early 1900s, when machines that could manufacture ice became common. Nevertheless, the ice trade demonstrated how a creative idea and patient testing could transform a winter resource into a global business.

Deep underground, some of the most remarkable landscapes on Earth are hidden in complete darkness. Limestone caves, with their long tunnels and enormous chambers, can stretch for many kilometers. Although caves may look as if they were carved by powerful tools, most of them were shaped gradually by something much gentler: water.

The process begins with rain. As rainwater falls through the atmosphere, it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide gas, and when the water soaks into the soil, it picks up even more carbon dioxide from decaying plants. The carbon dioxide combines with the water to form a weak acid called carbonic acid. This acid is far too mild to harm a person, but it has an important effect on one particular kind of rock.

Limestone is composed mostly of a mineral called calcite, which slowly dissolves in carbonic acid. As acidic water moves downward through small cracks in limestone, it dissolves a thin layer of rock along the way. Over thousands of years, the cracks widen into narrow passages, and eventually some passages become large enough for a person to walk through. The largest caves may require millions of years to develop.

Once a cave has formed, water continues to change it, but in a different way. When water drips from the ceiling of a cave, it carries dissolved calcite with it. Inside the cave, some of the carbon dioxide escapes from the water into the air. As a result, the water can no longer hold all of its calcite, and a tiny amount of the mineral is left behind. Drop by drop, these deposits accumulate. Formations that hang from the ceiling like icicles are called stalactites, while those that rise from the floor, where the drops land, are called stalagmites. When a stalactite and a stalagmite finally meet, they form a column.

These formations grow extremely slowly; in many caves, a stalactite may gain only a centimeter or so in a hundred years. For this reason, scientists can examine cave formations to learn about the past. Layers inside a stalagmite, much like the rings of a tree, can reveal how much rain fell in the surrounding area long ago.

Because they take so long to form, cave formations are easily damaged and nearly impossible to replace. Even the natural oils from a single human hand can prevent a formation from growing in the location where it was touched. Consequently, many caves that are open to visitors have designated paths and railings, and guests are instructed never to touch the walls or formations. By following these regulations, visitors help protect features that nature required thousands of years to create.

Today, it seems natural that everyone in the same region sets their clocks to the same time. Yet for most of history, this was not the case. Until the late 1800s, nearly every community kept its own time, and this system functioned reasonably well until a new form of transportation made it confusing.

In the past, people set their clocks according to the sun. When the sun reached its highest point in the sky, it was noon. Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the sun reaches this position slightly earlier in towns to the east and slightly later in towns to the west. As a result, when it was noon in one city, it might be 12:10 in a city to the east and 11:50 in a city to the west. This method, known as local solar time, caused few difficulties when most people traveled by horse or on foot, because a journey between two towns took so long that a difference of a few minutes hardly mattered.

The railroads transformed this situation. By the middle of the 1800s, trains could carry passengers hundreds of kilometers in a single day. Each railroad company usually established its schedules according to the time in its home city, so travelers had to deal with numerous different times at once. In the United States alone, there were more than fifty different railroad times. A train station might display several clocks on the same wall, each showing a different hour. Passengers frequently missed connections, and in the worst cases, confusion about schedules contributed to accidents when two trains used the same track.

To solve the problem, railroad leaders in the United States and Canada agreed on a new plan. On November 18, 1883, they divided the continent into a small number of time zones. Within each zone, every clock would display the same time, and neighboring zones would differ by exactly one hour. Some people called the event "the day of two noons," because many towns had to set their clocks back, and in those places the clocks struck noon a second time that day.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some people complained that the railroads had no right to control time, which they believed belonged to the sun, and a few cities refused to adopt standard time for years. Nevertheless, the system proved so useful that it spread. In 1884, representatives from many nations met in Washington, D.C., and selected a line passing through Greenwich, England, as the official starting point for measuring longitude. This decision helped establish the worldwide system of time zones that people rely on today.

choices: Why trains became faster during the 1800s
How people measured the position of the sun
Why and how standard time zones were created
How the city of Greenwich became famous
explanation: The passage explains the problems caused by local solar time and railroads, the creation of time zones in 1883, and their spread.

Today, it seems natural that everyone in the same region sets their clocks to the same time. Yet for most of history, this was not the case. Until the late 1800s, nearly every community kept its own time, and this system functioned reasonably well until a new form of transportation made it confusing.

In the past, people set their clocks according to the sun. When the sun reached its highest point in the sky, it was noon. Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the sun reaches this position slightly earlier in towns to the east and slightly later in towns to the west. As a result, when it was noon in one city, it might be 12:10 in a city to the east and 11:50 in a city to the west. This method, known as local solar time, caused few difficulties when most people traveled by horse or on foot, because a journey between two towns took so long that a difference of a few minutes hardly mattered.

The railroads transformed this situation. By the middle of the 1800s, trains could carry passengers hundreds of kilometers in a single day. Each railroad company usually established its schedules according to the time in its home city, so travelers had to deal with numerous different times at once. In the United States alone, there were more than fifty different railroad times. A train station might display several clocks on the same wall, each showing a different hour. Passengers frequently missed connections, and in the worst cases, confusion about schedules contributed to accidents when two trains used the same track.

To solve the problem, railroad leaders in the United States and Canada agreed on a new plan. On November 18, 1883, they divided the continent into a small number of time zones. Within each zone, every clock would display the same time, and neighboring zones would differ by exactly one hour. Some people called the event "the day of two noons," because many towns had to set their clocks back, and in those places the clocks struck noon a second time that day.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some people complained that the railroads had no right to control time, which they believed belonged to the sun, and a few cities refused to adopt standard time for years. Nevertheless, the system proved so useful that it spread. In 1884, representatives from many nations met in Washington, D.C., and selected a line passing through Greenwich, England, as the official starting point for measuring longitude. This decision helped establish the worldwide system of time zones that people rely on today.

Goal: In this investigation, you will find out which of three common solids dissolve in water.

Many of the world's first cities developed beside rivers. In ancient Egypt, people built towns along the Nile River, and in Mesopotamia, cities formed between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers. Why did early people choose these locations?

First, rivers provided fresh water for drinking, cooking, and washing. Second, rivers helped farmers. Each year, many rivers flooded, and when the water went down, it left behind a layer of rich, dark soil called silt. Crops grew well in this soil, so farmers could produce more food than their families needed. Extra food meant that not everyone had to farm, so some people could become builders, traders, or teachers.

Rivers also functioned like highways. Boats could transport heavy goods, such as grain and stone, much faster than people could carry them over land, which made trade between towns easier.

Of course, living near a river also had risks, since a flood that was too large could destroy homes and fields. Still, for early people, the benefits were greater than the dangers.

Along the Pacific coast of North America, underwater forests of kelp, a type of large brown seaweed, provide food and shelter for many species of fish, snails, and other organisms. The health of these kelp forests depends heavily on a small, furry mammal: the sea otter.

Sea otters consume large numbers of sea urchins, spiny animals that feed on kelp. When otters are present, they keep the urchin population under control, and the kelp can grow tall and dense. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, however, hunters killed sea otters in enormous numbers for their valuable fur. In many areas, otters disappeared completely. Without their main predator, sea urchins multiplied rapidly and devoured huge areas of kelp. Locations that had once been rich forests became "urchin barrens," rocky sea floors with little life.

After laws began protecting sea otters in the twentieth century, otters gradually returned to parts of their former range. Where they recovered, urchin populations declined and kelp forests began to regrow, bringing back many of the fish and other animals that depend on them.

Scientists describe the sea otter as a keystone species. Like the keystone at the top of a stone arch, which holds the other stones in place, a keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem that is much larger than its numbers would suggest. Removing it can cause the entire system to change.

During the 1930s, a series of severe dust storms struck the southern Great Plains of the United States, a region that included parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico. This area became known as the Dust Bowl.

The disaster had both natural and human causes. In the early 1900s, high wheat prices and new machines such as gasoline-powered tractors encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of grassland. The deep roots of native prairie grasses had held the soil in place for thousands of years. Once the grass was removed, the soil was exposed. Then, beginning in 1931, a long drought struck the region. Crops failed, and with nothing to anchor it, the dry topsoil was easily lifted by strong winds.

Some storms carried dust hundreds of miles, darkening skies as far away as the East Coast. Many families lost their farms, and hundreds of thousands of people migrated west in search of work.

In response, the federal government created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935. Its experts taught farmers methods such as planting rows of trees as windbreaks and plowing along the natural curves of the land. These practices reduced erosion, and when rain finally returned near the end of the decade, the land gradually began to recover.

Statistics appear constantly in everyday life, from news reports about home prices to announcements about average test scores. Two of the most common statistics are the mean and the median. Understanding the difference between them can help people interpret information more accurately.

The mean, often called the average, is calculated by adding all the values in a data set and dividing by the number of values. The median is the middle value when all the values are arranged in order from smallest to largest. In many data sets, these two numbers are fairly similar. However, they can differ significantly when a data set contains outliers, values that are much larger or smaller than the rest.

Consider a small company with five employees. Four of them earn $40,000 per year, and the owner earns $240,000. The mean salary is $80,000, which is twice what most employees actually earn. The median salary, however, is $40,000, which describes the typical worker much more accurately. A single high salary pulled the mean upward but had no effect on the median.

For this reason, economists usually report the median when describing incomes or home prices. Otherwise, a few extremely expensive houses or very high salaries could make an area appear wealthier than it actually is. Before drawing conclusions from a statistic, a careful reader should ask which measure is being used and whether outliers might be influencing it.
